newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - U.S. rail challenges barges for grain cargo.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - U.S. rail challenges barges for grain cargo.

text.p: Freight trains through the Pacific Northwest are challenging the traditional dominance of low-cost Mississippi River barges to haul Midwestern grain bound for Asian markets.

Thanks to bigger capacity railway cars, more efficient locomotive engines and cheaper labor costs, western railroads are now able to offer transportation rates that nearly match -- and may soon beat -- the cost of moving export grain down the Mississippi aboard barges, according to transportation experts.

And once the grain is delivered to a deepwater port in the Pacific Northwest, it has a 5,000-mile advantage over U.S. Gulf Coast ports in shipments to Japan and other Asian markets. The shorter distance means cheaper oceangoing freight costs.

"Western railroads are now actively pricing against barges on the Mississippi River, which they did not do as recently as two years ago," said Jerry Pinkepank, a consultant with the Transport Specialty Group in Seattle. "Rail costs have dramatically fallen."

The convergence of transportation costs of river barges and railroads gives more options to U.S. growers selling commodities to the booming markets of Asia, experts said at this week's meeting of the U.S. Feed Grains Council.
BRAZIL, ARGENTINA TO SLASH SHIPPING COSTS

A study of transportation costs, conducted for the feed grains group by private consultants and the U.S. Agriculture Department, shows that the emerging competition comes at a time when U.S. farmers are trying to trim export costs to compete with Brazil and Argentina for the fast-growing Asian grain market.
Preliminary results of the study were presented at the feed grain group's meeting in Philadelphia, and the final report is scheduled to be released in August.

Oceangoing transportation rates for grain exported from Parana, Brazil to southeast Asia -- currently at about $74 per tonne -- will plunge to about $39 per tonne by 2005, according to the study. The rate for shipping grain from Santa Fe, Argentina, to Asian markets is expected to similarly drop from $45 per tonne to about $35 per tonne during the same period.
Both countries will see savings from privatized railways, lower labor costs and greater efficiency.

By comparison, the cost of shipping grain from Iowa through the U.S. Gulf and then to Asia will remain stable at about $39 per tonne, the study found. And transporting grain from Nebraska through the Pacific Northwest and on to Asia will decline from a current average of about $49 per tonne to an estimated $42 by the year 2005.
U.S. RAILWAY COSTS DROP
As an example of the rapid changes in U.S. inland transportation, the study showed that Union Pacific's operating costs fell 20 percent per net ton mile between 1989 and 1996.

That reflects a reduction to two in the number of railway employees aboard each Union Pacific freight train, down from the union-required five employees a few years ago. Other savings were realized by replacing older locomotive engines with more efficient ones that burn less fuel, and from the merger of rail companies.

Together, those changes have dropped the cost of shipping export-bound corn from points in Nebraska, central Iowa and the upper Midwest to the Pacific Northwest by about 15 cents to 18 cents a bushel over the past two years, Pinkepank said.
A typical 108-car Union Pacific train bound for Portland or Seattle can come within five percent of the barge costs to move grain from St. Paul to Baton Rouge on a per net ton basis, he said.

Burlington Northern Santa Fe, which also links the U.S. prairie states and the Northwest, is making similar improvements. The railroad already helped eliminate bottlenecks caused by rough weather and flooded out tracks by opening a line through Stampede Pass in Montana.
BIGGER RAILCARS, BARGES COMING
But the biggest competitive impact may be yet to come.

After several years of analyzing the impact on tracks, Union Pacific is beginning to introduce larger, 115-ton capacity cars that can move more grain at roughly the same cost as the traditionally cheaper barge transportation. A 108-car train using the bigger cars could actually offer transportation costs two percent lower than barges, Pinkepank said.
Union Pacific has also earmarked some $700 million to improve freight service by adding double tracks and new rail sidings.
"We don't see a lot of potential for the Mississippi River barge system to improve its economics like the railroad system has," Pinkepank said.
But like the railways, some barge owners are also thinking bigger is better to trim costs and build economies of scale.

For the first time since the early 1980s, the five major U.S. barge companies are building large numbers of new vessels, many with a bigger capacity 14-foot draft rather than the traditional 12-foot draft. The 14-foot draft vessels can hold 2,200 tons of grain, about 400 tons more than existing barges.
The bigger barges came about after shippers saw a 30 percent increase in break-even costs on the Mississippi during the past five years, experts said.
By the end of 1998, the U.S. fleet of barges should number about 12,290, compared to 10,440 in 1993, according to Mark Fletcher, a shipping expert with Ceres Consulting.
"The shipping rates are going to converge," Fletcher added. "But there's still a question in my mind how efficient the railroads can get."
The five biggest barge companies -- American Commercial Barge Lines, Archer Daniels Midland Inc, Peavey, Midland and Cargill Inc -- account for more than half of the U.S. fleet of barges.
PACIFIC NW PORTS POISED FOR GROWTH
Ports in Seattle, Kalama and Portland are scrambling to build facilities to keep up with the growing shipments.

In 1995, about 24 million tonnes of U.S. grain moved by rail from the Midwest to the Pacific Northwest. By the year 2015, shipments should top 38 million tonnes, said John Fratt, executive director of the Port of Kalama on the Columbia River in Washington.

"We anticipate corn exports will surpass the volume of wheat exports shortly, particularly once ADM opens its new facility at the port of Longview," Fratt said. Corn bound for export could top 22 million tonnes at Pacific Northwest ports by 2015 versus just 13 million tonnes two years ago, he added.
But Midwestern farmers with easy access to the Mississippi won't be looking at alternative transportation, experts said.

"The infrastructure in New Orleans isn't going to go away. Those folks are going to compete for business," said Fletcher. "When barge rates are high, producers will rail west. And when barge rates are reasonable, the grain will go south on the river."
